title: Encoded but Not in Control: Revealing the Grounding Gap in Vision-Language Robot Policies
action_head: flow/diffusion action expert (pi0.5, GR00T N1.7 DiT); world-action models with video co-training (FastWAM, LingBot-VA autoregressive diffusion)
methods: scene-preserving instruction interventions (in-scene target replacement, random noun, random sentence)
layerwise 'action lens' (apply action readout to intermediate states)
linear probes for target and scene identity on instruction tokens
question: When a VLA succeeds, is it following the instruction or inferring the task from the scene, and if language is encoded, why does it fail to control target selection?
key_findings: In LIBERO-Object target replacement, 86.5-98.3% of trials go to the original (scene-associated) target and only 0.5-13.0% to the newly instructed one; current-target success 0.0-11.5% (Table 1).
Real robot: pi0.5 picks the original target in 74.2% vs 5.8% for the instructed one; GR00T N1.7 90.8% vs 3.3% (Table 1).
Language still matters: random sentences cut LIBERO-Goal success from 98.0 to 11.7% (pi0.5) and 97.5 to 4.0% (GR00T); random nouns have smaller, task-dependent effects (Table 2).
Action lens: random sentences shift intermediate action predictions most, then in-scene replacements, then out-of-scene nouns, with separation growing at later denoising steps (Fig. 2).
Target and scene identity are linearly decodable from mean-pooled instruction-token representations at 96-100% before and after fine-tuning (Fig. 3).
Instruction tokens get a small share of attention-value contribution to action tokens: pi0.5 25.6-27.9% on LIBERO, ~1.7% on RoboTwin, 9.7% real world; GR00T 18.5-23.4%, ~12%, 13.5%.

After fine-tuning, pi0.5 instruction representations cluster by scene rather than target in middle layers (UMAP), and all 12 shared NMF components shift toward scene-unique variance from layer 2 onward.

evidence.scale: RoboTwin: 100 rollouts per task; LIBERO per-model protocols with matched seeds across instruction conditions; representation sets of 60 (LIBERO-Object) and 36 (real) scene-target instances; action lens from one successful rollout per model; real-world trial counts not stated in main text
evidence.statistics: no: percentages only, no CIs or tests
evidence.baselines: original instruction condition; base vs fine-tuned checkpoints for probes/UMAP/NMF

causal_validation: Input-level interventions only (changing the instruction with the scene fixed) with behavioral and action-lens readouts. No activation patching, ablation or steering, and the authors say the representational analyses do not establish a causal mechanism.
closed_loop: Yes for behavioral results (closed-loop sim and real robot). The action lens and probes are open-loop on recorded states.
limitations_stated: Representational analyses (attention contribution, UMAP, NMF) are consistent with the behavior but do not establish a causal link.
Action-lens deviations show sensitivity, not movement toward the instructed target.
critique: The '100% target decodability' probe reads mean-pooled instruction tokens, which literally contain the target noun. Decoding it is trivial and says nothing about whether the target is grounded in the visual or action pathway. A probe on action-expert tokens or visual tokens would be the informative test.
Attention-weighted contribution is a correlational proxy; a modality-ablation or patching experiment on instruction tokens would turn the 'weak contribution' claim into a causal one.
No CIs or rollout counts in the main text for the key target-replacement table, although the effect sizes (86-98% vs 0.5-13%) are large enough that the conclusion is unlikely to flip.

The behavioral finding reproduces earlier counterfactual-instruction results (LIBERO-CF, LangGap) and 2608.13474's appendix; the new part is extending it to world-action models and the real robot, plus the scene-vs-target reorganization after fine-tuning.
The headline is consistent with 2609.34684 and 2607.03372: decodability is cheap and does not imply use.
one_line: With the scene fixed, pi0.5, GR00T and two world-action models almost always grab the object their training scene implies rather than the newly instructed one, even though the instruction is encoded and does perturb the computation; fine-tuning reorganizes language representations around scene identity.
